analysis.one_liner: Rolls insulin list prices back to 2006 levels and bans insurer and middleman rebates on that insulin.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to slash insulin list prices was referred to the Finance Committee in July 2019 and never received a markup or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill offered insulin manufacturers a deal: if a maker voluntarily cut its insulin's list price back to what it charged on July 1, 2006, that insulin would be 'certified,' and insurers and pharmacy benefit managers would be barred from taking back-end rebates on it. Certified insulin could not be subject to a deductible, and insurers and middlemen could not drop it from formularies, raise cost-sharing, or add prior-authorization or step-therapy hoops for two years. The price cap would then rise only with the medical care component of the Consumer Price Index. It also applied to Medicare Part D plans and pegged Medicaid rebates to 2019 price levels so government programs wouldn't lose rebate payments when list prices fell.
analysis.who_benefits: People who use insulin — especially uninsured patients and those in high-deductible plans, who pay list price or full deductible amounts out of pocket. Insulin list prices roughly tripled in the years after 2006, and cash-pay patients bore the brunt. For them, a certified insulin at 2006-era list prices, exempt from deductibles, would mean a direct and large cut in out-of-pocket costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insulin users, especially uninsured and high-deductible patients

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers who certify would have to cut the list price of an insulin to no more than its July 1, 2006 level, and could raise it afterward only by the annual increase in medical-care inflation.

Once insulin is certified, insurers and pharmacy benefit managers may not receive back-end rebates or discounts on it, and any price reduction must be reflected at the point of sale so the patient sees it at the counter.
Plans could not apply a deductible to certified insulin, and the bill amends the tax code so plans that exempt insulin from deductibles still qualify as high-deductible health plans.

For the first two years after certification, insurers and PBMs could not remove certified insulin from formularies, raise its cost-sharing, or impose new prior-authorization or step-therapy requirements.

The same rebate ban and hold-harmless rules apply to Medicare Part D prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans, and Medicaid rebates would be calculated from pre-cut 2019 prices so states and the federal government don't lose rebate dollars when list prices fall.
Health and Human Services' Inspector General could audit manufacturers' price data, with civil penalties for knowingly submitting false or incomplete data.

analysis.who_pays: Insulin manufacturers give up roughly thirteen years of list-price increases on any insulin they certify and their ability to trade list-price inflation for rebate deals. Pharmacy benefit managers and insurers lose the rebate stream on certified insulin, and plans must absorb insulin outside their deductibles.

drawbacks.text: Participation is voluntary: a manufacturer can simply decline to certify and keep its current high list prices and rebate arrangements, so the bill guarantees cheaper insulin only for makers who take the deal.

The deal trades away the rebate system rather than attacking prices directly, and the certified price floor rises with the medical care component of the Consumer Price Index, which has historically grown faster than overall inflation, so allowed price increases would outpace general inflation.
The formulary, cost-sharing, prior-authorization, and step-therapy protections last only the first two plan years after certification, after which plans could re-tighten access.

Manufacturers with no 2006 list price for a product (such as newer insulins) certify against a weighted average of 2006 category prices, a benchmark set by data submissions and HHS rules rather than a direct historical price, which relies on the accuracy of manufacturer-submitted data.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly seven million Americans who depend on insulin, the potential gain was large and direct: list prices cut by more than half for certified products, with no deductible standing in the way. The design's honest weakness is that it is an invitation rather than a mandate — every manufacturer had to choose to accept a major revenue cut — and the enforcement of the price data behind the certifications depended on audits and penalties after the fact. It was a narrower tool than a direct price cap, but a real one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced by a bipartisan group of four senators, referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day, and never received a markup, hearing action, or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jeanne Shaheen introduced the Insulin Price Reduction Act on July 22, 2019, joined by Senator Susan Collins, Tom Carper, and Kevin Cramer, giving it two Democratic and two Republican original supporters.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced; no further action appears in its history for the remainder of the Congress.

The bill would have let manufacturers voluntarily certify insulin at July 2006 list prices, banned back-end rebates on certified insulin by insurers and pharmacy benefit managers, barred deductibles on certified insulin, and applied equivalent rules to Medicare Part D and Medicaid.
It drew three cosponsors — two Republicans and one Democrat — beyond Shaheen, and the Senate took no recorded vote on it at any point.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insulin manufacturers, pharmacy benefit managers, and insurers kept the existing rebate-based pricing system intact, and patients continued to face the inflated list prices and deductible barriers the bill would have removed. Insulin prices have since fallen through separate mechanisms, including cap-shot programs and later legislation, not this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers, PBMs, and insurers kept the status quo

for.name: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Insulin Price Reduction Act and recruited a bipartisan group of cosponsors.

for.name: Sens. Susan Collins, Tom Carper, and Kevin Cramer
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors, making the bill bipartisan from introduction.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — two Democrats and two Republicans among the original sponsors — so the bill's death in committee was not a party-line vote; it simply never came to one.

industries.industry: Insulin manufacturers (Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, Sanofi)
industries.note: Certifying would have cost manufacturers roughly thirteen years of list-price increases and their rebate deals, but in exchange they would gain a regulated price floor rising with medical inflation, freedom from rebate negotiations, and a hold-harmless guarantee of formulary placement. Their existing pricing model — high list prices funding back-end rebates — is what kept insulin out of reach for uninsured patients, so their interest ran against the patients this bill served.

The bill bars PBMs from receiving back-end rebates on certified insulin, allowing only point-of-sale discounts and transparent flat service fees. PBM compensation is built on negotiating and capturing those rebates, so the bill directly attacks that revenue stream.

Insurers would lose rebate revenue on certified insulin and could no longer count insulin against deductibles, though they would also pay less at the counter. The bill's point-of-sale discount exception lets patients capture savings immediately rather than through plan-year rebates.
